cards.title: AOSP Source Releases Are So Late Developers Disassemble Libraries to Report Bugs

depth.text: Android's **text search** mistakes **non-ASCII characters** for matches, and someone **traced the bug** in shipped code

On Android 17 builds from September 2026, wcscspn() and wcspbrk() stop at the first character at or above U+0100 when the reject set has two or more characters, all below U+0100. A sweep returned the wrong result for **1,111,808 code points**. The report used **disassembly** to trace it to the shipped libc.so; public Android 17 source showed **different code**, prompting complaints about delayed AOSP releases.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say the unavailable current source makes it hard to inspect what ships; others say this bug could be reported without disassembly, which was only extra root-cause work.

comments.text:

I can't remember which one it was, but one of the recent regulations mandates that devices get updates for a certain period. Within that period a manufacturer must provide each update for all their devices in a short timeframe. The intention was to prevent flagships getting updates immediately…

One character: a plain compare loop. Correct. Not surprisingly, I get slight hints of Claudism in the text. AI "opening" the source of software is one of the best things I've seen going for it so far.
The new Google motto seems to be "be as evil as you can". We need an Android alternative, something that respects users' freedom.

We need a third option. Be it SalfishOS, Ubuntu Touch, Nura, or whatever picks up with a sizable community. We just need to start developing and investing in that one. It won't be perfect, but it will offer an alternative and control to the users.

Bit of a hyperbolistic title. The core of the bug report doesn't require disassembly of the library. The bug author just went the extra step to do a root cause investigation, which of course requires light reversing work.

cards.title: Iosevka is an open-source, sans-serif and slab-serif, monospace font

depth.text: Iosevka is a **coding font** with **narrow letters** and lots of ways to customize its look

Its monospace glyphs are exactly **1/2em wide** by default, letting more columns fit on screen. It has Term and Fixed families for terminal users, plus **146 configurable characters** and **19 stylistic sets**.

cards.camps: Two camps: fans praise its compactness and customizability; one commenter dislikes code ligatures because some symbols are hard to tell apart.

comments.text: IMO a font specimen site may be the worst place to use font-display: swap. Was wondering why I was looking at what seemed indistinguishable from Courier, turns out what I saw was exactly Courier.

Iosevka, my absolutely most loved font for years! I've been using a custom version - you can customize the font¹ and build your own ttf (or better yet, ttc) using the build system supplied in the repository². be5invis, the author of the font, deserves a special mention for creating a whole custom DSL called PatEL (Parametric Type Expression Language) to generate the font programmatically! Renzhi…

First time I used Iosevka I felt really nauseated, kind of like getting motion sickness, it was a really bizarre experience for a font to give me. I was on a smaller screen though and getting some more characters in without getting tiny was actually a selling point, so I gave it another go and eventually got over the feeling. Now (after ... gosh, 6, 7, 8? years probably) I love it, use it…

Have been using it for a couple years. Before that I was using Fira Code/Mono which was also fantastic. However, once I got used to the condensed Iosevka, all the other fonts just felt loose and not space efficient enough in my IDE and terminal.

cards.title: Recreational Programming

depth.text: someone makes the case for **coding for fun**, with **small experiments**, personal tools, and **no need for a payoff**
It suggests spending **2-4 hours** exploring one new thing, building toy versions of tools you use, or explaining a project as you build it. Abandoned repos count as **exploration, not failure**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some celebrate coding for its own joy; others say making software that people value feels more fulfilling. Commenters also split on AI, with some finding it helps them build and others feeling existential about programming as a hobby.

The author recommends **seeded randomness** and save/load so agents can recreate exact states, then using **image diffs** to check changes. **Replayable commands** let agents test game actions without compiling.

cards.title: Chapter 1 of "Ways of Seeing" by John Berger (1972)

depth.text: John Berger argues that **how we see art** changes when **images are copied** and moved around
He says reproductions make a painting's meaning **multiply and fragment**. He argues that original works are treated like **holy relics**, with market value presented as spiritual value.

cards.camps: Two camps: fans recommend Berger’s book and series; critics call it hard to digest or incomprehensible, and say its Marxism spoils everything.
entities: The Virgin and Child with St Anne and St John the Baptist

cards.title: MIT class project turns into an FDA-cleared treatment for tremors

depth.text: an **MIT class project** became an **FDA-cleared wristband** that uses vibrations to help adults with tremors

Encora’s watch-like product sends **mechanical vibrations** from the wrist; trials with 47 and 59 patients found **more than 70 percent** experienced meaningful improvement. The FDA gave it **510(k) clearance** to help adults with essential tremor.
data: Patients with meaningful improvement in both trials

cards.camps: Some commenters are excited about another option for essential tremor; another says FDA clearance only means the device is similar to an already approved one, not that the FDA tested or approved it.

comments.text:

- the device doesn't stop the tremors
- the pulsed vibration does let the brain's control signal come through stronger, so…

cards.title: Cyberattack halts construction of tunnel between Denmark and Germany

depth.text: a **cyberattack** stopped work on a **tunnel** linking Denmark and Germany

Workers’ **identification cards** stopped functioning, while vessels, cranes and platforms used for offshore work were **immobilized**. Who was behind the attack and how long it will take to eliminate its consequences are still **unknown**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters warn AI could bring more cyberattacks; others say incidents like this may come from basic, exposed systems rather than AI.

comments.text: Big picture, where this leads is a lot of physical stuff just getting unplugged from the Internet. It's very easy to see how this goes — one side of the ledger is the cost savings you get from remote monitoring, remote control, automated cloud backups of access logs from employee badges, or whatever dumb reason this system was internet-connected in the first place. On the other side of the ledger…
Danish source: https://www.dk-sundhed.dk/ritzau/1f0b6211-3397-4869-98aa-a2e...

AI will exponentially increase the number of cyberattacks. The likely outcome is 1. Legacy firmware will be a bloodbath, leading to a consolidation of firms 2. All digital infrastructure will have an always on AI "shield" of agents that monitor and defend against attacks 3. The attacks that survive will depend on human points of failure, leading to less control for humans being the default

Karpathy yesterday posted [1] about the gap between small % of population getting high leverage from AI, and the rest of the world. We have a much more urgent gap between software powering the "physical world", and the digital natives. The digital natives now have 10x leverage with AI, with the ability to rapidly find and deploy exploits. We're now seeing a lot of this - fridges defrosting…
The internet became a single point of failure for all of civilization years ago and we're only realizing it now.

glossary.AOSP: Android Open Source Project: the publicly available base software people can use to build Android systems.
glossary.NDK: Native Development Kit: Android's tools for making apps with code that talks directly to the device.
glossary.ASCII: American Standard Code for Information Interchange: an older character set for basic English letters, numbers, and punctuation.
glossary.libc: A basic library of common functions that programs can call instead of building everything themselves.
glossary.disassembly: Turning a finished program into a readable list of steps so someone can inspect how it works.
glossary.wcscspn(): A text-search function that counts characters until it hits one from a stop list.
glossary.reject set: A list of characters the search is supposed to stop when it finds.
glossary.code point: A number assigned to a character, such as the value written as U+0100.
glossary.monospace: A font where every character takes the same width, so text lines up in columns.
glossary.quasi-proportional: A font where some letters can be wider or narrower than others.
glossary.glyph: A character or symbol as it appears in a font.
glossary.ligature: A special shape a font uses for a set of letters, sometimes replacing them with one different shape.
glossary.stylistic set: A group of alternate letter designs that you can turn on together.
glossary.OpenType: A font format that lets a font include extra options, like alternate letter shapes.
glossary.intrinsic motivation: Wanting to do something for its own sake.
glossary.ROI: Return on investment: a way to ask whether what something achieves is worth what it costs.
glossary.repo: A project's stored files, often kept with a record of changes.
glossary.CLI: Command-Line Interface: a way to control a computer by typing commands instead of clicking buttons.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.ray tracer: A program that makes images by working out how light would bounce around a scene.
glossary.Electron: A tool for making desktop apps with web technologies, so a web-style app can run like a regular computer program.
glossary.Flash: A technology used to make games and animations that played in web browsers.
glossary.tokens: Small pieces of text an AI counts as it reads or writes; they can affect how much a request costs.
glossary.UI-maxxing: User interface maxxing: slang for going all-in on making a screen feel elaborate or flashy.
glossary.DEI: Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion: efforts to make groups and workplaces fairer and more welcoming to people who have been left out.
glossary.operating expenses: The regular bills an organization has to pay to keep running.
glossary.colour swatch: A small sample of a colour, used to compare or identify it.
glossary.colour theory: Ideas about how colours work together and how they can be mixed.
glossary.high-resolution scan: A detailed digital copy that stays clear when you zoom in.
glossary.long s: The old-fashioned form of the letter s that can look like an f.
glossary.Math.random: A command in JavaScript that gives a program a number that looks random.
glossary.RNG: Random number generator: a tool or program that produces numbers meant to seem unpredictable.
glossary.mod: A way to keep only the remainder after dividing one number by another.
glossary.harness: The surrounding code that gives an AI agent tools and a place to work, and checks what it does.
glossary.seeded randomness: A way to make random choices repeat the same sequence, so a game can return to a testable state.
glossary.image diffing: Comparing two images to show which parts changed.
glossary.deterministic state: A game situation you can recreate exactly, so repeated tests start from the same place.
glossary.command pattern: A way to save an action as an instruction you can replay, instead of changing the game directly.
glossary.mystification: Explaining something away in a way that hides what might otherwise be clear.
glossary.perspective: A way of drawing things so they seem to get smaller with distance, arranged around where the viewer stands.
glossary.Marxism: A political way of looking at society that focuses on class, wealth, and who holds power.
glossary.510(k) clearance: An FDA route for allowing a medical device on the market when it is similar to an existing device.
glossary.essential tremor: A condition that causes shaking, often in the hands.
glossary.FDA: Food and Drug Administration: the US agency that oversees food and drug rules, including food labeling.
glossary.hybrid warfare: Using things like sabotage and disinformation to pressure or weaken another country.
glossary.air gapping: Keeping a computer or network physically disconnected from the internet and other networks.
glossary.Shodan: A search engine people use to find devices connected to the internet.
glossary.hardcoded login: A username and password built into a device’s software, rather than something users can easily change.
glossary.APT: Advanced Persistent Threat: an attacker that keeps trying to get into computer systems over time.
